chapter.title: What a Portal Is
chapter.description: Rendering into a different DOM node while staying in the React tree.

blocks.text: `createPortal` renders children into a DOM node somewhere else in the document, while keeping them exactly where they are in the React tree.

A modal or tooltip nested deep inside the page inherits its ancestors' CSS. `overflow: hidden` clips it, a `transform` traps `position: fixed`, and a low `z-index` on an ancestor puts it behind other content. No amount of styling on the modal itself can escape those.

items: `overflow: hidden` on any ancestor clips the popup.
A `transform` or `filter` on an ancestor makes it the containing block for `position: fixed`.
Stacking contexts mean a child can never rise above a sibling of its ancestor.

blocks.text: This is the part that surprises people. A portal's DOM node is elsewhere, but events bubble up the **React** tree, not the DOM tree - so a click inside a portal reaches handlers on its React parent.
This catches people building click-outside handlers: a click inside a portalled dropdown still bubbles to the React parent, so a naive 'close when anything is clicked' handler closes immediately.
Because the component stays in the React tree, it keeps access to every context and every error boundary above it. Portals change the DOM position and nothing else.

next.title: Building an Accessible Modal
next.description: The parts a portal does not give you for free.

blocks.text: A portal solves the layout problem. Accessibility is a separate job, and a modal that skips it is unusable with a keyboard or a screen reader.

items: `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` so assistive technology announces it correctly.
Focus moves into the dialog on open, and back to the trigger on close.
Focus is trapped inside while it is open - Tab must not reach the page behind.
A click on the overlay closes; a click inside does not.

blocks.text: Focus trapping is fiddly to get right. The native `<dialog>` element handles much of it, and libraries such as Radix UI or React Aria handle all of it. Write one by hand once to understand the requirements, then use a tested implementation.

blocks.caption: A dedicated container is easier to style and to reason about than document.body.
